To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the liver cell contains at least two systems for the transport of Ca2+; one of them, the Ruthenium red-insensiive transport system is present in the microsomes (endoplasmic reticular membranes) and is the system that responds to the administration of glucagon.
the initial rate of ruthenium Red-insenstive Ca(2+) transpo is enhanced by 2- to 3-fold by glucagon administration to adult rat liver.

Ruthenium Red (RR)-insensitive Ca2+ transport activity, which is maximal at birth, remains so for up 10 weeks of post-natal life, and is increased in the intermediate but non-microsomal fraction in response to the administration of glucagon in adult rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a study of the subcellular location of Ca(2+) and glucose transport activities in rat liver, their development during maturation and the effect of hormones on these activities.
the elucidation of the role of the endoplasmatic reticulum in the liver cell in the control of the intracellular concentration of Ca(2+) and the effect of glucagon on this process.
the role of Ca2+ as a second messenger in the control of liver function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hormone-sensitive Ruthenium Red insensitive Ca(2+) transporting system is a component of the endoplasmatic reticulum of the liver cell.

the hormone-sensitive Ruthenium Red insensitive Ca(2+) transporting system is located in the intermediate fraction and that the hormone-induced stimulation of this system is an essential part of glucagon's metabolic action in liver.
Ruthenium Red insensitive Ca(2+) uptake in the liver is a microsomal phenomenon and the system is activated by glucagon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
glucagon, in addition to its known effects on glucose metabolism and on the release of Ca(2+) from the microsomal Ca(2+) stores, is also able to enhance the uptake of Ca(2+).

the liver cell has a system of Ruthenium-Red-insensitive Ca(+) transport activity, which is located in the endoplasmatic reticulum and responds to glucagon administration in a manner similar to that of glucose-6-phosphatse.

the hormone-induced effects on the transport are mediated through an increase in the number of the transport units, the increase in the number being due to an increase in the synthesis of the protein(s) concerned.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the glucagon effect is not a simple one, and it is not clear that the effect on the microsomal Ca(2+) pump is a direct one.
glucagon has an effect on Ca(2+) homeostasis in the liver cell that is independent of that of the Ca(2+) pump.
the Ca2+-ATPase activity of the ER is a major contributor to the Ca2+ homeostasis of the hepatocyte.
